narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. While the average third-year ranking among accepted students is nearly 5.8, you placed in the 4th decile. This weaker performance in your final undergraduate year signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your first-year ranking was the next most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure, though less strongly. At 6.0, it matched the average of accepted students, yet still contributed to the overall risk assessment.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. Scoring 38.5, which is slightly above the 37.2 average of accepted applicants, this result helped push the prediction toward passing and reduced the estimated risk. However, it was not enough to overcome the negative impact from your later academic performance.

The model did not consider your gender, race, family income, undergraduate GPA, or planned full-time status in reaching this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening skills tested on the bar exam. Consider retaking the LSAT for a higher score, enrolling in a rigorous bar-preparation course, or gaining additional academic experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas that most influenced the current decision. (248 words)
